The fluorescent lights of Ward Seven hummed with an oppressive constancy, casting their sterile glow across the cracked linoleum floor. Dr. Elias Finch stood in the doorway of Room 4B, his white coat immaculate, his expression professionally neutral despite the weight of the morning. Before him sat Patient 027—Marcus Webb—perched on the edge of his cot like a crow on a telephone wire, dark eyes gleaming with that familiar unsettling intelligence. The small paper cup with two blue pills sat on the metal tray between them, untouched.

***

"It's time for your medication, Marcus," Dr. Finch said, his voice measured and calm, the same tone he'd used for the past three years. "You know the routine." Marcus didn't move. Instead, he tilted his head, a slow smile spreading across his gaunt face, the kind of smile that made the hairs on Dr. Finch's neck stand at attention. "How do I know they're safe, Doctor?" Marcus whispered, his voice like dry leaves skittering across pavement. "How do I know you're not trying to poison me? You've been watching me. I see you watching."

***

Dr. Finch sighed, pinching the bridge of his nose. This was the game they played—had always played—the endless circuit of paranoia and professional patience. "Marcus, we've been through this. The medication helps you. It quiets the voices, the visions. You've told me yourself that you feel better when you take them." But Marcus was shaking his head now, his smile widening into something almost grotesque. "You take them," he said. "You take them and prove to me they're safe. Then I'll take mine."

***

Something flickered in Dr. Finch's chest—frustration, yes, but something else too, something he couldn't quite name. He glanced at the pills, then back at Marcus. It was against every protocol, every rule he'd been taught. And yet... what harm could it do? They were just antipsychotics, low-dose, nothing that would hurt him. Perhaps this was the breakthrough he'd been waiting for, the moment when Marcus would finally trust him. "Fine," Dr. Finch said, reaching for the cup. "I'll take them. And then you'll take yours. We have a deal."

***

The pills were bitter on his tongue, dissolving with a chemical taste that made him grimace. He swallowed hard, chasing them with nothing but his own saliva, and held out his hand to show Marcus the empty cup. "There," he said. "Satisfied? Now it's your—" But the words died in his throat. He blinked once, twice, the fluorescent lights suddenly too bright, too sharp. The edges of the room seemed to waver, like heat rising off summer asphalt. And Marcus—Marcus was laughing, but the sound was wrong, distant, like it was coming from the end of a very long tunnel.

***

Dr. Finch closed his eyes against the dizziness, against the strange pulling sensation in his skull. When he opened them again, the room was empty. The cot was made, crisp and untouched. The metal tray sat bare, no paper cup, no pills. There was no Marcus Webb. There had never been a Marcus Webb. The realization crept over him like ice water, and he looked down at his own hands—trembling, pale—and saw the patient wristband on his own wrist, the number 027 staring back at him. Somewhere down the hall, a door clicked shut, and a voice that was his own and not his own whispered: "See, Doctor? I told you they were safe."
